lead: Continuous integration (CI) means every developer merges into the shared mainline at least daily, and every merge is proved by an automated build and test run. Continuous delivery keeps that mainline always releasable, so shipping is a business decision, not an engineering scramble. Continuous deployment sends every passing change to production automatically. The idea exists because late integration gives 'it works on my machine' surprises and long release nights. It is used wherever software ships often — a UPI app, an IRCTC booking service, a cloud product.
prereq: You need: 5.5 Version control systems, because a push to the mainline is the trigger, and 5.3 Test automation, which supplies the tests the pipeline runs.

sections.h3: Integration, delivery and deployment are three different promises

blocks.text: Continuous integration (CI) is a practice: every developer merges into the shared mainline at least once a day, and every merge is checked by an automated build and an automated test run. The mainline is the one branch the team shares. When the check fails, fixing it is the team's first job; a red mainline blocks everybody.

Integration is the hard part. Two branches kept apart for three weeks touch the same files, and someone must resolve the conflict by hand. Daily merges keep the difference small, so conflicts stay small too.

Continuous delivery means every change that passes the pipeline leaves the mainline releasable today. Which release goes out, and when, stays a business decision. Continuous deployment removes that decision: every passing change reaches production automatically.
A deployment pipeline is the automated path a commit walks from push to production. Each stage is a check; stages run in fixed order and stop at the first failure.

items: Commit: a developer pushes to the mainline; the push is the trigger.
Build: compile and link, or build a container image; a broken build stops everything in minutes.
Unit tests: seconds to minutes; catch most logic errors.
Integration and acceptance tests: slower tests against a real database or service; split into parallel shards when they dominate the time.
Package: write the artifact (jar, war, image) to an artifact repository under a unique version.
Deploy to staging: an environment that mirrors production.
Smoke tests: a short check that staging serves its main paths.
Deploy to production, with automatic rollback if health checks fail.

blocks.text: Two rules make a pipeline useful. Fail fast: run the cheapest, fastest checks first, so a typo is caught in two minutes, not forty. Build once and promote: the artifact tested on staging is the one copied to production. A rebuild means you released something nobody tested.

blocks.where: T is pipeline wall-clock time in minutes; the sum runs over stages; t₁ … tₖ are run times in minutes of the k jobs running in parallel inside one stage, and max picks the longest.

sections.h3: Practices that keep the mainline releasable

items: Trunk-based development: branches live hours or a day, not weeks, and merge back to the trunk.
Pipeline as code: the pipeline definition is a file in the repository (Jenkinsfile, .gitlab-ci.yml, .github/workflows), reviewed and versioned like code.
Environment parity: staging has the same operating system, database version and configuration as production; every difference hides a defect.
Versioned database migrations: schema changes are scripts in the repository, applied by the pipeline, never typed by hand on a server.
Immutable artifacts: the same stored file moves from stage to stage, so staging and production run identical bytes.

blocks.text: DevOps is the culture and tooling that removes the wall between development and operations: one team owns the code, pipeline and running service. Jenkins, GitLab CI and GitHub Actions run build and test stages; Argo CD keeps a cluster in sync with the repository. Most pipelines run in the cloud, where a fresh test machine is minutes of provisioning, not a purchase order.

Blue-green release: two identical environments, blue serving live traffic and green receiving the new version. When smoke tests pass, the router points at green; rollback points it back at blue in seconds.

Canary release: a small slice of traffic, for example 5% of requests, goes to the new version while the rest stays on the old one. If error rates rise, the canary is withdrawn before most users notice.

Feature flags separate deploy from release: code ships dark and a switch turns it on for chosen users. A flag lets unfinished work merge to the trunk safely. Rollback needs the previous artifact kept and one command to restore it; a pipeline that cannot roll back is not a delivery pipeline.

figure.caption: The 26-minute pipeline: four integration shards finish in 5 minutes instead of 20; the last stage is the release gate that must not be deleted.

spec.aria: A twenty-six minute pipeline: build 0 to 5, unit tests 5 to 13, four parallel integration shards 13 to 18, package 18 to 21, staging deploy 21 to 23 and smoke tests 23 to 26 minutes.

examples.question: A team's pipeline runs stages in series: build 5 min, unit tests 8 min, integration tests 20 min, package 3 min, deploy to staging 2 min, smoke tests 3 min. (a) Find the total wall-clock time. (b) Integration tests are split into 4 equal parallel shards; find the new total. (c) Unit tests are then split into 2 equal shards; find the new total. (d) A manager suggests deleting the smoke stage instead. Comment with numbers.
steps: The pipeline time is the sum of stages because each waits for the one before it (T = Σ max(t₁ … tₖ) with one job per stage).
(b) Shard length = 20 ÷ 4 = 5 min. New total = 5 + 8 + 5 + 3 + 2 + 3 = 26 min. Saving = 41 − 26 = 15 min.
(c) Unit shard length = 8 ÷ 2 = 4 min. New total = 5 + 4 + 5 + 3 + 2 + 3 = 22 min, a further saving of 4 min.
(d) Deleting smoke gives 26 − 3 = 23 min, saving 3 min, less than the 4 min won by sharding unit tests. It also removes the only check on deployed staging, so refuse; parallelise first, delete never.
examples.answer: 41 min in series, 26 min with four integration shards, 22 min after also splitting unit tests into two; the 3-minute smoke stage stays because it is the release gate.
examples.check:
build, unit, integ, pkg, stage, smoke = 5, 8, 20, 3, 2, 3
serial = build + unit + integ + pkg + stage + smoke
print(serial)
shards = 4
shard = integ // shards
print(shard)
parallel = build + unit + shard + pkg + stage + smoke
print(parallel)
unit_shard = unit // 2
print(unit_shard)
faster = build + unit_shard + shard + pkg + stage + smoke
print(faster)

traps: Saying 'we do continuous integration' because a Jenkins server exists, while branches live for weeks. The practice is a daily merge into one green mainline.
Treating continuous delivery and continuous deployment as the same. Delivery means every change is releasable and a person chooses the moment; deployment ships without asking.
Rebuilding for production instead of promoting the tested artifact. The binary you release is then not the binary you tested.
Making the pipeline fast by deleting acceptance or smoke tests. Shorten by sharding and parallelising; a removed gate releases defects.
Reading fail fast as test less. It means cheapest checks run first so failure is reported in minutes, not that later checks are dropped.

quiz.q: Define continuous integration in one sentence.
quiz.a: Every developer merges into the shared mainline at least daily, and every merge is checked by an automated build and test run.

quiz.q: State the difference between continuous delivery and continuous deployment.
quiz.a: Delivery: every passing change is releasable, and a person decides when. Deployment: every passing change goes to production automatically.

quiz.q: Why does a three-week-old feature branch make integration harder than a one-day branch?
quiz.a: It has diverged further: more files overlap the mainline, conflicts are larger and manual, and its defects stay hidden from the team until merge.

quiz.q: Stages run in series: build 3 min, unit tests 6 min, integration tests 12 min, package 2 min, deploy to staging 2 min, smoke tests 1 min. Find the total, then the total after splitting integration tests into 3 equal parallel shards.
quiz.a: Series total = 3 + 6 + 12 + 2 + 2 + 1 = 26 min. Shard length = 12 ÷ 3 = 4 min. New total = 3 + 6 + 4 + 2 + 2 + 1 = 18 min, saving 8 min.

quiz.q: A team runs a Jenkins job that builds the mainline once a week, while developers keep branches for three weeks. Does the team practise continuous integration? Justify.
quiz.a: No. CI requires merging into one mainline at least daily and keeping it green after every merge. A weekly build of a mainline most work never touches proves nothing about integration; conflicts will be large and late.

quiz.q: Why build once and promote the same artifact rather than rebuild for production?
quiz.a: A rebuild can pick different dependencies, compiler settings or base images, so production runs bytes never tested. Promotion keeps staging and production identical and rollback exact.

quiz.q: A service cannot be stopped for even a minute. Which release technique do you choose, and how does rollback work?
quiz.a: Blue-green. Blue serves live traffic while green receives the new version. When smoke tests pass, the router switches to green, so no outage. Rollback switches back to blue, which still holds the previous version.

quiz.q: How does a feature flag support trunk-based development?
quiz.a: Unfinished code merges to the trunk daily behind a flag switched off in production. The mainline stays releasable, small merges keep conflicts small, and deploy is separated from release without a long-lived branch.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industry extends this with GitOps, where a repository is the source of truth for code and cluster state, reconciled by Argo CD or Flux. Supply-chain security adds signed artifacts, a software bill of materials and provenance checks. Teams track deployment frequency, lead time, change failure rate and time to restore to judge whether the pipeline helps. Progressive delivery adds automatic canary analysis.
